claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in Cr- and Ta-containing refractory high-entropy alloys is due to a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer.
The high-entropy matrix slows elemental diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion causes selective enrichment of Cr and Ta at the alloy surface.
Cr and Ta have high oxygen affinities.
Surface-enriched Cr and Ta react to form a stable CrTaO4-based oxide.
The CrTaO4-based layer acts as a kinetic barrier to oxygen ingress and slows further oxidation.
The initial material is a homogenized, single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy with no pre-existing oxide scale.
Isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours is an applicable test condition for the proposed CrTaO4-forming alloy.
Comparing a full-Cr/Ta alloy with a reduced-Cr/Ta variant under identical oxidation conditions would test the proposed role of Cr and Ta.
The structural mediator is a dense, continuous CrTaO4-based surface layer.
The integrity of the CrTaO4-based layer is maintained by sluggish diffusion inherent to the high-entropy matrix.
Without sluggish diffusion, selective oxidation would be less efficient and the resulting scale would be porous and non-protective.
The full-Cr/Ta alloy will form a well-adhered oxide scale.
The oxide scale will begin as a laminated mixed-oxide layer and transition into a continuous CrTaO4-based layer.
At 1100 °C, formation of the protective CrTaO4-based layer will be associated with parabolic oxidation kinetics and low mass gain.
The full-Cr/Ta alloy will have significantly lower mass gain than a reduced-Cr/Ta control alloy.
A reduced-Cr/Ta control alloy will form a porous, non-protective scale and exhibit exponential mass gain.
The proposed behavior applies to refractory high-entropy alloys during prolonged oxidation around and above 1000 °C.
Grain coarsening, phase segregation, very high oxygen pressure, or corrosive atmospheres may alter the oxidation kinetics or destabilize the protective scale.
Failure of the full-Cr/Ta alloy to show both lower mass gain and a distinct continuous CrTaO4-based layer relative to the reduced-Cr/Ta control would falsify the hypothesis.
